svg.aria-label: A lesson on light: the lamp, your own mix, two beams, a wall, filters, two slits, your screen.

g.text: Light
On a screen, a colour is three numbers: how much red, green, and blue to
light. A picker, a palette, a photo editor: every colour tool edits those three
numbers. The numbers are not the start. The start is light from a lamp. The
eye reads the light, reduces it to three numbers, and drops everything else at
that step. This page is one step earlier. The light itself is in the code on the
left, and the page computes the colour from it at the end, by the same
reduction the eye makes. The step matters: two paints can be one colour
under a shop lamp and two colours in daylight. The reason is in the light, and
it is gone from the three numbers. You can edit any number in the code. The
page computes every picture below from that code, and the judge re-checks
it as you type.
The setup
The lamp is glowing hydrogen, the simplest atom there is. Sunlight through a
glass prism is a rainbow. The lamp’s light through the same prism is no
rainbow: only a few thin stripes of colour. Those stripes are called lines.
Three of hydrogen’s lines are written in this file: a red one, a blue-green one,
and an infrared one that eyes cannot see: the light of TV remotes.
the lamp
Hβ 486 nm
Hα 656 nm
infrared 1875 nm
beyond the eye
The three lines are the atom’s own: for hydrogen there are only these three.
Other gases have other lines, and the three squares below are hydrogen,
neon, and sodium at full: the page computes each from its own list.
hydrogen
neon
sodium
The middle square is the light of a neon sign. The right one is a sodium
streetlight.
In the code, each of the three lines has one brightness number.
Mix your own beam
The keys set each line’s brightness, 0 to 8. The square is the computed
colour of your mix.
Hα 656 nm
Hβ 486 nm
infrared 1875 nm
your beam
The infrared key changes the code, and the colour is unchanged: press it and
see.
The gas is one line of code: these keys rewrite it, the page redraws.
hydrogen lamp
neon
sodium
The colour map
To the right the red level is higher, downward the blue-green. The ring is on
your mix.
The infrared has no direction on this map: raise it, and the ring is where it
was.
Two beams, one colour
BeamX is the red line alone. BeamY is the red line and the infrared one. The
eye adds up only what it can see, so both squares below are the same. The
two paints under the shop lamp are the same case: one sum from two
different lights.
the eye sees
the page computes both squares from the code on the
left
BeamX
BeamY
The black windows are a prism’s view: it spreads a beam into its lines.
The visible lines are the same, the difference is only in the infrared, and the
judge checks both sums equal: the squares must be the same. A colour
picker stores only the sum. This code has both beams.
Press Raise IR: the page draws the line longer, and the squares are
unchanged.
Raise IR
Lower IR
Break it: set AlphaLevel in BeamY to Lit2. The judge names the difference.
A wall and a mirror
A matte wall keeps only the total of the light and drops the side it came from.
A room lit from the east and the same room lit from the west are the same on
the wall. A mirror keeps the two sides apart.
The judge checks the two readings equal. The direction numbers are still in
the code: FromEast and FromWest are separate lines there.
Break it: set LitFromWest’s Total to Lit2. The judge refuses the claim.
Three filters
Light is a wave, and a wave has a direction of vibration. A polarizing filter
admits only the light along its own direction, so two crossed filters admit
nothing: try it with two pairs of sunglasses. A third filter between them at 45
degrees, and the light is back.
two filters, crossed
from the lamp
past both filters
with the diagonal between
from the lamp
past the diagonal
at the screen
The screen below is live. The filters are crossed: it is dark.
the screen now
Insert the diagonal
Remove it
You brought the light back through more glass than before.
The 2 on the screen is not measured: half of a half is in the code, and the
judge checks it. A typical simulator would get 1.9999 and round. Here the 2 is
exact. None of this fits in a colour: its three numbers are three brightnesses.
Break it: set the diagonal Vertical to Lit1. The judge refuses both rows.
Two slits
The sum of two lights can be darkness. The scene here is a lamp behind two
slits in a wall, and a screen in front. Each spot of the screen is lit twice by the
lamp, once through each slit. The two paths are different lengths, and the
difference is in half-steps. With an even gap the two arrivals are in step: the
spot is bright. With an odd gap they are opposite: the spot is dark.
The stripes are the four written gaps, 0, 1, 2, and 3 half-steps, and the page
reads each at the edge. The judge checks each gap’s parity: the darkness is
arithmetic, not a measurement.
The stripe below is live: its gap is the LiveGap line in the code.
Widen the gap
Narrow it
Each press of a key is one half-step of the gap. Even is bright, odd is dark.
Break it: in NodeFirst, make Gap even. The judge refuses the stripe’s claim.
What your screen can show
This code has colours your screen cannot show, and you can check that on
this page. Every screen has a standard: sRGB is common, P3 and Rec.2020
are wider. Two pairs of red and one lone square are below. In each pair both
squares are equally bright, and only the purity of the red is different.
sRGB and P3
P3 and Rec.2020
the lamp’s line
On a screen too narrow for the difference, a pair is one colour. On most
screens the first pair is two colours. The second is two only on a very wide
screen.
The lone square is the lamp’s pure line. No screen can show that colour, so
what you see there is your screen’s closest colour to it.
You can write a screen’s limit as a rule, and a red-green screen is in this
code: yellow fits it, red and green lit and blue dark, and the claim is clean. A
pure blue does not fit: instead of clipping it, the judge refuses it and names
the blue channel.
Break it: set YellowAtFull’s BlueChannel to Lit1. The judge names the blue
channel.
The eye tells apart only finitely many colours, so a complete list of them is
one file. An eye would tell every pair above apart: the limit is the screen’s.
What is different here
A colour picker stores three numbers, and the parts of the light are gone. A
simulator computes and rounds, and you check its output by eye. The light
itself is in this code, the judge re-checks it as you type, and the judge checks
a filter chain of your own the same way.
